turns.content: For x^2 + 7, exhibit a representation as a sum of squares of polynomials in Q[x] that gives an upper bound for the smallest possible number of summands.

To test whether four summands could suffice, allow zero terms and write f_i(x) = a_i x + b_i for i = 1, ..., 4. Justify the degree bound and compare coefficients to obtain the equations for the rational numbers a_i and b_i.
Use positive-semidefinite Gram factorization and real matrix rank, allowing real factors, as the sole method for determining the minimum number of squares.
For the rational descent, set p_i = a_i + b_i and q_i = a_i - b_i. Use the coefficient equations to compute sum p_i^2, sum q_i^2, and sum p_i q_i.
Choose a positive common denominator m for all p_i and q_i, clear denominators, and state the resulting three equations for integers x_i = m p_i and y_i = m q_i.
Prove the needed parity fact for four integer squares whose sum is divisible by 8, and apply it to the two square-sum equations to determine the parity of every x_i and y_i.
Use the dot-product equation to determine the parity of m. Then show how dividing x_i, y_i, and m by 2 would produce another solution of the same integer system.
Explain why choosing a solution with the smallest positive m makes the descent from the previous step impossible, and state what this proves about a four-square representation over Q[x].
Combine that obstruction with the explicit construction from the first step to determine the smallest possible n.
